national.title: NASA's Voyager 1 calls Earth from more than 16 billion miles, or one light-day, away
national.summary: It marked another day in the history books for Voyager 1, which launched in 1977.
national.body:
CAPE CANAVERAL, Fla. (AP) — NASA's Voyager 1 has phoned home from one light-day away, humanity's first emissary to cross this monumental threshold way out in interstellar space.

Flight controllers received the spacecraft's call Thursday, exactly 24 hours after it was sent. That's how long it took for the radio signal to traverse the more than 16 billion miles (26 billion kilometers) at the speed of light.

"Traveling a light-day is a singular feat for a spacecraft, but Voyager is so much more than a distant traveler," NASA's Joe Westlake, the heliophysics division director, said in a statement.

It marked another day in the history books for Voyager 1, which launched in 1977. It swept past Jupiter in 1979 and Saturn in 1980, snapped the most distant photo ever taken of our "Pale Blue Dot" in 1990, became the most distant human-made object in 1998, and crossed from the sun's sphere of influence into the vast void between stars in 2012.

NASA could not confirm this newest distance record until the signal reached the control team at California's Jet Propulsion Laboratory. But that didn't stop the space agency from wishing everyone a "Happy Voyager light-day … day!" via social media the day before.

"Voyager 1 crossing the light-day threshold is yet another historic feat on an extraordinary voyage of discovery," JPL director Dave Gallagher said in a statement.

Voyager 1 and its twin, Voyager 2, are NASA's longest-operating space missions, still churning out data despite powering down most of their instruments to keep exploring.

Voyager 2 actually beat its twin into space by two weeks. But its route to Jupiter and Saturn plus Uranus and Neptune was slower and longer, and it did not reach interstellar space until 2018. It won't reach the one-light-day mark until 2035.

national.title: Kushner says Russia is 'comfortable' with NATO-like security guarantees for Ukraine to end war after Trump talks with Putin
national.summary: Ukrainian officials fear their country's fate could be determined by agreements between Trump and Putin, raising concerns among European governments.
national.body:
Hanna Arhirova, Associated Press Hanna Arhirova, Associated Press

Barry Hatton, Associated Press Barry Hatton, Associated Press

BERLIN (AP) — U.S. envoy Jared Kushner on Thursday said Russia is "comfortable" with NATO-like security guarantees for Ukraine to end the war as it nears the five-year mark.

Another American envoy, Steve Witkoff, said U.S. President Donald Trump discussed Ukraine and a peaceful end to the war during his trilateral talks with the Russian and Chinese leaders earlier Thursday.

Kushner and Witkoff met with European allies in Berlin to discuss their support for Ukraine after a third Ukrainian aerial attack in four days on the key Kerch Bridge linking Russia to Russian-held Crimea halted rail traffic across the span, officials said Thursday, after earlier strikes shut down the road section of the landmark that is a symbol of Moscow's invasion.

Train traffic across the bridge stopped after the overnight strike while authorities assessed the damage, but it resumed in the afternoon, according to Russian state news agency RIA Novosti.

The Ukrainian strikes seemed calculated to embarrass Russian President Vladimir Putin as he met in China with President Xi Jinping and Trump, as well as to demonstrate that Kyiv still holds cards in the war and to undermine Russia's argument that its victory is inevitable.

The attack came hours before the start of talks in Berlin between Kushner, Witkoff and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy alongside more than 40 European leaders who are supporting Ukraine's war effort and fear being sidelined by Trump's direct talks with Putin.

national.title: CBS to air Kennedy Center Honors in December
national.summary: CBS has reached a one-year deal to air the awards ceremony next month, sources said.
national.body: The Kennedy Center Honors may have left the Kennedy Center itself, but the annual awards gala isn't leaving its longtime broadcast home. CBS has reached a one-year deal to air the awards ceremony next month, according to sources familiar with the arrangement. This year's event, scheduled to be taped on Sunday, Dec. 7, and aired on Dec. 27, will be held at Capital One Arena in downtown Washington. Honorees include musicians Paul Anka and Barbara Mandrell, composer David Foster, actor Andy Garcia and playwright David Mamet.In September, the Kennedy Center board voted to close the performing arts center amid a legal dispute over building upgrades and attempts to add President Trump's name to the facade. Mr. Trump said he would only help fundraise for renovations if his name was added to the facade. A federal judge in Washington, D.C., however, ruled that only Congress had the authority to change the building's name. While modest maintenance projects continue, planning for the major renovations are underway and a construction schedule cannot be set until an ongoing federal court case halting construction is resolved. A court hearing is set for Thursday. CBS has broadcast the Kennedy Center Honors each year since 1978. The multiyear contract lapsed after the 2025 show, but the arts center and the network reached a short-term deal for this year's show last week. The program will also stream on Paramount+.President Trump co-hosted the show in 2025, punctuating artistic performances with several speeches throughout the evening. The White House did not respond to a CBS News inquiry on whether the president would attend this year.

national.title: The 'Magic Six': How to strengthen your marriage in midlife
national.summary: How do we maintain healthy romantic relationships as we age? Allison Aubrey and Scott Detrow talk about about the science of healthy, later-in-life relationships.
national.body:
Ever argued with your spouse in the car? NPR's Nina Totenberg can relate.

She and her husband, David Reines, have been married for 26 years, and it's on the road where they're most likely to have a spat. "The car is awful," Totenberg told me, laughing. It comes down partly to the brakes. She taps them "way before" Reines does. And when another driver cuts him off, he sometimes wants to return the favor. Totenberg's advice from the passenger seat: "Don't take the bait."

It's so relatable. And as Reines put it, "You can't not have some conflict after 26 years. I think the secret is how you deal with it." (They began our interview for this episode of Your Turn by giving each other a kiss!)

As we ask "What comes next?" in midlife, who's standing beside us matters a lot. Kids leave home, careers shift, and relationships can change, too. So what does a good partnership look like at this stage?

When people ask Reines why their marriage works, he points to four L's:

Like. Do you actually like each other? For Reines, respect is part of this. He says he has total respect for her work, and she respects his career, too. He is a retired trauma surgeon and now keeps busy as a volunteer at the Library of Congress and serves on boards. Each of them also keeps a strong sense of self. "Although we meld," Reines says. "I still have me , and she still has her ."

Lust. Physical intimacy matters. They kiss every day, hold hands, "all the time," and have held off on buying a king-size bed. In hotel beds, they joke, they can't find each other if the bed is too big.

Laugh. He says she has one of the best senses of humor he knows. They laugh together every day.

national.title: Are tech disruptions and and outages the new normal?
national.summary: The Trump administration maintains there is "zero" indication that the latest outages are linked, or caused by bad actors like cybercriminals.
national.body:
Wyatte Grantham-Philips, Associated Press Wyatte Grantham-Philips, Associated Press

Kaitlyn Huamani, Associated Press Kaitlyn Huamani, Associated Press

Inaccessible email inboxes. Banking delays. And a communications meltdown that grounded airplanes for hours, followed by waves of other travel disruptions.

In an increasingly interconnected world, some fear such disruptions could be the new normal.

Over the past week alone, problems that appeared to emerge from routine updates, security patches or other malfunctions surfaced at Microsoft, JPMorgan Chase and Apple, and even the U.S. government's Federal Aviation Administration and National Security Agency. The Trump administration said there was "zero" indication the latest outages are linked, or caused by bad actors like cybercriminals.

The era of artificial intelligence has also raised the stakes for internet security overall. As AI tools uncover new vulnerabilities, many other companies and institutions are racing to patch them before they can be targeted by hackers, a cat-and-mouse game that can lead to a different set of glitches.

Social media platforms have been abuzz with a mixture of annoyance, confusion, conspiracy theories and jokes about the string of outages.

"To see several disruptions this close together, I think to a lot of people it's made them realize how many parts of their lives they've handed over to these systems that we still, at this point, don't fully understand," Jake Smith, a content creator who regularly posts videos about politics on platforms like Instagram and YouTube, said in an interview. "I think it gives people a sense of helplessness to see all of it happening concurrently in a way."

national.summary: Deirdre Keane, a 38-year-old nurse and management consultant, achieved her goal of completing all seven World Marathon Majors while pregnant with her first child.
national.body: Deirdre Keane had already run more than 60 marathons when she decided to take on a new challenge of completing the World Marathon Majors. She just didn't expect to be running them while pregnant.Earlier this month, the 38-year-old nurse practitioner and management consultant ran the New York City Marathon — her hometown race — in her third trimester. It was the seventh marathon she finished while pregnant and the final race she needed to achieve her goal of running all the Majors in the same year. In addition to New York, the other marathons in the premier series are Berlin, Boston, Chicago, London, Sydney and Tokyo.Keane completed the New York City Marathon in just over 4 hours, with an average mile pace of 9 minutes, 26 seconds, according to New York Road Runners, the group that organized the race. She had completed the same marathon in just over three hours in 2025, records show."I knew how bizarre it was to be running a marathon at 34 weeks, but I also knew how fit I was and self-aware of my body at this point," Keane told The Associated Press. "And while it is very unusual, I wasn't the first woman to have ever done this."Keane, who has completed 74 marathons and ultramarathons, received clearance from her doctor to compete in the races, as long as she remained vigilant about nutrition, hydration and stopping exercise at the first sign of muscle cramping, the World Running Network reported. That advice worked for Keane because she was already such a highly trained athlete."My last hurrah"After getting married last year, Keane and her husband Brian began talking about starting a family. Expecting pregnancy to take a while, Keane made other plans for herself in the interim."In my mind, 2026 was going to be my year of bucket list items," Keane recalled. national.title: Analysis: Trilateral summit high on spectacle, short on substance
national.summary: The visuals of the historic trilateral meeting may be the only lasting impression left by the summit.
national.body:
Donald Trump went into his trilateral meeting with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping with little on the agenda and no clear asks – and it appears that he left with little in return.

In the end, the visuals of the meeting – the "optics", as political wags like to say – may be the only lasting impression from the summit, billed by some as an historic "Yalta 2.0" meeting of great powers.

The pomp and the ceremony, in the end, may be what the US president wanted most. Trump, bruised by his Republican Party's drubbing in midterm congressional elections earlier this month, clearly relished the global spotlight during his three-day trip to Asia and the historic nature of the first-ever US-Russia-China trilateral meeting.

Trump, Putin and Xi release 'peace declaration' after historic meeting

Published 1 hour ago This is a remarkable diplomatic moment for China's Xi - but it comes with pitfalls

Published 14 hours ago In an interview on Wednesday with Fox News, Trump noted his prominent seat at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) dinner on Tuesday and his reception upon arriving in China - "the fanfare, the beauty, the pageantry, the thousands of people" – as evidence that the trip already was a success.

That might appear to be a low bar, but it's one that could satisfy the American president.

So far, however, the US has been remarkably silent following the three-party meeting.

national.title: Trump, Putin and Xi release 'peace declaration' after historic meeting
national.summary: While the presidents have previously met for one-on-one meetings, this is their first trilateral discussion.
national.body:
US President Donald Trump and his Russian and Chinese counterparts Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping have issued a "joint declaration of peace" following historic trilateral talks.

The three leaders met for 90 minutes in China's south-eastern city of Shenzhen, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit.

While the presidents have previously had one-on-one meetings, these are their first trilateral talks.

In the declaration, they said "nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought" and that the countries planned to increase the production and supply of petroleum. They also said they were "committed to reform the UN" to respond more effectively to global challenges.

Thursday's statement also flagged the issue of immunity enjoyed by state officials and said "they agreed that the International Criminal Court and other similar institutions must not abuse their jurisdiction".

Trump praised the trilateral meeting calling it "a great and highly consequential trip", in a social media post while flying back to Washington on Air Force One.

In the same post, the president announced he would host a news conference to talk about the trip on Friday at the White House.

While in China, Trump met Putin ahead of the trilateral, in their first meeting since August 2025, where the US president greeted his Russian counterpart as his "friend".

national.summary: The verdict marks the first time a state has ever been found to have committed genocide by an international court.
national.body:
Rohingya genocide: What was said in court and what happens now? Close Myanmar has been found guilty of committing genocide against its Rohingya minority by the International Court of Justice (ICJ).

The verdict marks the first time a state has ever been found to have committed genocide by an international court.

The court found on Thursday that "genocidal intent is the only reasonable inference that can be drawn from the evidence" it had seen.

The verdict was reached by a majority of nine votes to six among a panel of judges from around the world.

The BBC's Anna Holligan is in the Hague and reports on what the ICJ's ruling means.

national.title: Susan Smith denied parole again 32 years after drowning her two sons
national.summary: At a hearing on the possibility of parole, Smith said she wished she could change the past, and her two children "did not deserve to die".
national.body:
A South Carolina woman who admitted to drowning her two sons 32 years ago has been denied parole for a second time.

Susan Smith, 55, was convicted of killing her boys by strapping them into their car seats and rolling her vehicle into a lake in 1994.

"I got to my lowest when I let that car go into that lake," Smith said during a hearing on Thursday with the state board that decides whether to release those in prison on parole.

The seven-member board later unanimously turned down her request to be freed. The father of the two boys has vowed to continue to oppose her release, and several people spoke against her in the hearing.

Smith, whose lawyers had argued she suffered a mental breakdown during the crime, can apply to the South Carolina Board of Probation, Parole and Pardon Services for parole every two years.

She told the board that she had changed and matured since killing three-year-old Michael and one-year-old Alex, and that "I am not the same person I was 32 years ago".

She also said she was "very, very sorry" and that she would go back and change the circumstances if she could.

"They were innocent children," Smith said. "They did not deserve to die."

national.title: Putin says Russia won't negotiate with Ukraine after bridge strike
national.summary: Russian President Vladimir Putin said Russia will not negotiate any limited ceasefire now with Ukraine, citing a Ukrainian strike on a highly symbolic bridge this week.
national.body: President Vladimir Putin said Thursday that Russia will not negotiate with Ukraine on a limited ceasefire, citing a Ukrainian strike this week on a major bridge connecting Russia and Ukraine's Russian-occupied Crimean Peninsula. Putin made the remarks to reporters in Russian after meeting with President Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen, China. He said he had discussed the possibility of a ceasefire in certain areas of Ukraine, but would not move forward with negotiations after Ukraine's strike on the Kerch Bridge, according to the Russian state news agencies. The 12-mile bridge, which Putin ceremonially opened himself in 2018, is hugely symbolic as it links the Russian mainland with Crimea — territory that Russian forces occupied about four years earlier. The missile strike this week wasn't the first time Ukraine had targeted the piece of infrastructure, but it inflicted severe damage. Russia also struck two major bridges in Kyiv the same day. Putin played down the bridge's strategic importance on Thursday and said he had heard the calls "from all sides" for a naval ceasefire or a suspension of strikes on energy facilities, but he ruled out direct negotiations with Ukraine, citing the attack on the bridge."Honestly, I discussed the issue with my colleagues at the Security Council, and I asked them to think about it and go back to the issue, so that we could reach some agreements," Putin said, according to Russian state news agency TASS. "However, we will not make agreements after strikes on the Crimean Bridge. We will respond to these strikes."Putin vowed that Russia's retaliation for the strike on the bridge would be severe, TASS reported. While Putin claims frequently to want peace, he denies that Russia started the war with his order for a full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, and Russia's attacks on Ukraine have been relentless. national.summary: Russia says Putin, Trump and China's Xi agreed during a rare meeting to boost gas and oil production, and "reaffirmed that there can be no winners in a nuclear war."
national.body: President Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin sat down together in Shenzhen, China, on Thursday in a rare face-to-face encounter for the leaders of three of the world's most powerful countries, but there appeared to be little concrete to show for the meeting in terms of resolving any of the crises facing the world.The leaders offered a joint statement after their roughly hour-and-a-half-long meeting. Mr. Trump immediately left for his return flight to the U.S. without speaking to journalists on the ground. On the flight home, the president said on social media he will hold a press conference at noon on Friday to discuss the trip.The presidents discussed Russia's ongoing war in Ukraine, which Mr. Trump has wanted to bring to a negotiated end. But the only significant statement on the conflict came after the meeting from Putin, who ruled out any direct negotiations with Ukraine, citing a major strike earlier this week by Ukrainian forces on a key bridge in Russian-held Crimea. Putin's senior aide Yuri Ushakov told reporters after the meeting that the atmosphere had been good, and the Kremlin quickly released what it called a joint statement from all three leaders characterizing the talks. national.title: 'I'm not MAGA,' Elon Musk says after Republicans' midterm thrashing
national.summary: Musk told The New York Times' DealBook Summit audience Wednesday he feels foolish for spending so much on the midterms.
national.body:
ATLANTA (AP) — Elon Musk was on the front row at Donald Trump's second inauguration and has spent hundreds of millions of dollars trying to help the Republican president and his "Make America Great Again" allies win elections.

Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News

Now, after Republicans' midterm thrashing by Democrats, the world's richest man insists he's not a MAGA acolyte after all and feels "pretty foolish" for spending so much money on the cause.

"I mean, I'm not MAGA," Musk told The New York Times on Wednesday during the newspaper's DealBook Summit.

"I'm not sure what MAGA means," the Tesla and SpaceX CEO continued, "but I, I don't think I'm, like, if, if that means sort of blind adherence to a set of policies by the Republican Party, then I certainly don't have that. I think there are, there, there are positives and negatives in both parties."

Musk, who has based himself and several of his companies in Texas, spent more than $400 million on Trump-aligned Republicans running in November. That included around $200 million backing Texas Senate nominee Ken Paxton, who lost to Democrat James Talarico.

Democrats scored sweeping victories after making Musk, other tech titans and the proliferation of artificial intelligence and AI data centers a feature of the midterm campaigns. Their party will take control of Congress and many more U.S. statehouses in January, with a promise of a regulatory crackdown and congressional investigations into tech firms' dealings with the Trump administration.

That leaves Musk and others scrambling to rebrand themselves after spending years aligning closely with Trump and his fellow Republicans as they sought government contracts and favorable policies on everything from taxation to AI regulation.

national.title: Iowa residents asked to evacuate Friday ahead of Army detonation
national.summary: The Army plans to detonate 68 barrels of degraded lead azide in Middletown, Iowa, at noon Friday. Forecasts show a dust plume moving north and staying west of the Chicago area, but sampling will determine where lead lands.
national.body: A plume of dust containing toxic lead particles is expected to spread across portions of eastern Iowa and northwest Illinois Friday, potentially settling on farmland, playgrounds and other surfaces, following a planned U.S. Army detonation of unstable explosives.The detonation is scheduled for noon CT Friday, Nov. 20, at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa, a small community of 360 people four hours west of Chicago near the Mississippi River.The Army plans two controlled detonations involving 68 barrels of lead azide, a highly sensitive explosive used in military ammunition since World War I. The Associated Press reported the material totals about 5 tons. According to the Environmental Protection Agency, the material has deteriorated during storage, allowing lead azide to recrystallize and become increasingly sensitive to friction and shock.The barrels had been stored at the plant for more than 20 years in earthen-covered containers, sitting in a bath of ethanol and water to keep the material stable, said Justine Barati, a public affairs specialist at Army Sustainment Command. national.title: Israeli military completes ground operation in Gaza beyond Yellow Line
national.summary: Hamas condemned the incursion, which the Israeli military said was to dismantle a "terror tunnel", as a "flagrant" ceasefire violation.
national.body:
Israeli forces have completed a rare ground operation in part of central Gaza outside their control, the military says, a day after residents were ordered to evacuate.

Families fled their homes and tents on Wednesday as tanks advanced into an area east of Nuseirat refugee camp and onto the territory's main north-south road under the cover of artillery strikes.

The Israeli military said the "targeted" operation aimed to dismantle a "terror tunnel" west of the so-called Yellow Line, which marks the more than 60% of Gaza's territory occupied by Israel.

The Palestinian armed group Hamas, which controls the rest of Gaza, accused Israel of a "flagrant violation" of the October 2025 ceasefire deal.

Violence has continued in Gaza over the past 13 months, with near-daily Israeli strikes, and living conditions for the 2.1 million people there remain dire.

Wednesday's Israeli incursion deep beyond the Yellow Line was reportedly the first to be publicly announced by the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) since the ceasefire began.

In the early afternoon, Israeli military body Cogat's Arabic spokesperson announced the start of the operation and warned Palestinians living in an area north of Nuseirat and Bureij refugee camp to stay away for their own safety. It also said a section of Salah al-Din road that passed through the area would be closed to traffic.

In the evening, the IDF said the joint operation with the Shin Bet security service sought "to dismantle a terror tunnel west of the Yellow Line that posed an immediate and direct threat to IDF troops".

national.title: Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya minority, top UN court rules
national.summary: The unprecedented International Court of Justice verdict concerns a 2017 military crackdown that killed thousands.
national.body:
Myanmar has been found guilty of committing genocide against its Rohingya minority by the International Court of Justice (ICJ).

The verdict marks the first time a state has ever been found to have committed genocide by an international court.

Yuji Iwasawa, president of the UN's top court, said Myanmar had the "intention to destroy" a substantial part of the Rohingya population and engaged in "extensive destruction of evidence" to hide its crimes.

A military crackdown in 2017 killed thousands of Rohingya and forced more than 700,000 to flee Buddhist-majority Myanmar, formerly known as Burma. Myanmar denied the claims against it, saying its forces had responded to attacks by armed groups.

The court found on Thursday that "genocidal intent is the only reasonable inference that can be drawn from the evidence" it had seen.

The verdict was reached by a majority of nine votes to six among a panel of judges from around the world. The ICJ also found in favour by majority that Myanmar had violated several other parts of the 1948 Genocide Convention.

The case brought by The Gambia centred around so-called "clearance operations" initiated in 2017 in Rakhine State, where many of the Rohingya Muslim minority resided.

After fighters from the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army (Arsa) launched deadly attacks on more than 30 police posts there, Myanmar troops, backed by local Buddhist mobs, launched a wave of violence, prompting a mass exodus of Rohingya.

national.title: For Putin, sharing a spotlight with Trump and Xi boosts his profile on the global stage
national.summary: For Russian President Vladimir Putin, Thursday's three-way meeting with Donald Trump and Xi Jinping offered a much-coveted chance for the Kremlin leader to demonstrate that he heads a superpower on a par with the United States and China.
national.body:
Vladimir Isachenkov, Associated Press Vladimir Isachenkov, Associated Press

For Russian President Vladimir Putin, Thursday's three-way meeting with Donald Trump and Xi Jinping offered a much-coveted chance for the Kremlin leader to demonstrate that he heads a superpower on a par with the United States and China.

While dealing another blow to Western efforts to isolate Putin, it also gave him an opportunity to try to persuade Trump to lean into Moscow's demands for a settlement in Ukraine at a time when Washington wants to broker a peace deal.

Putin said afterward that the meeting showed that the three-way format was "useful and substantive" and marked "serious joint work," including discussions on Ukraine. Earlier Thursday, Trump and Putin also met separately.

Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News

Kyiv and its European allies viewed the meeting on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China, with deep suspicion. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has said Europeans feared another "Anchorage moment," a reference to a Putin-Trump meeting in Alaska in August 2025 that produced proposals that were rejected by Ukraine and its partners.

Putin said Thursday that Russia accepted what he described as a U.S.-proposed compromise in Anchorage, declaring that Ukraine and its European allies would better accept it now or face tougher demands.

The three-way meeting raised comparisons to the 1945 Yalta conference, where the wartime leaders of the U.S., Britain and the Soviet Union divided Germany and Berlin, carved out zones of influence in Europe, and agreed to establish the United Nations. The Kremlin, which long has courted the concept of a "multipolar world" offering an equal say to all nations, plays down the Yalta parallels, which also are unwelcome to China for similar reasons.

JUNEAU, Alaska (AP) — Republican U.S. Rep. Nick Begich has won reelection to Alaska's lone U.S. House seat, hanging on during a year that saw Democrats regain control in both houses of Congress.

national.title: UN's highest court finds Myanmar responsible for genocide in historic ruling
national.summary: In a landmark judgment, the United Nations' top court ruled Thursday that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya minority in a brutal 2017 military operation and ordered the Southeast Asian nation to allow people who fled the violence to return home.
national.body:
THE HAGUE, Netherlands (AP) — In a landmark judgment, the United Nations' top court ruled Thursday that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya minority in a brutal 2017 military operation and ordered the Southeast Asian nation to allow people who fled the violence to return home.

The decision marks the first time the court has ruled that a state committed genocide and comes as the World Court also is handling genocide allegations linked to the Gaza conflict and the war in Ukraine.

But it remains to be seen how much of the ruling can be implemented. The court's rulings are final and legally binding, but it has no way to enforce them beyond reporting noncompliance to the U.N. Security Council.

Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News

International Court of Justice President Yuji Iwasawa said the court, in a 9-6 decision, found that Myanmar "has committed genocide against the Rohingya group in northern Rakhine state, in violation of its obligations under the Genocide Convention."

The 15-judge panel of the World Court, which included Navi Pillay , the respected international jurist who won the Nobel Peace Prize last month, rejected Myanmar's defense that the 2017 campaign was a legitimate operation against insurgents.

Iwasawa said that "the court finds that Myanmar's security forces killed thousands of Rohingya civilians, perpetrated widespread acts of sexual violence, as well as acts of extreme violence against children, and attacked fleeing Rohingya as they sought to flee in large numbers."

The atmosphere following the hearing was electric, with lawyers and members of the Rohingya, some of whom had traveled thousands of miles (kilometers) to attend the reading, hugging and crying.

national.title: The midterms were the largest win for either party in 50 years
national.summary: Some 56% of people cast votes for Democrats in House races, compared to 42% who voted Republican. That 14-point spread is the widest win for either party in 50 years, since after Watergate.
national.body:
With vote counts concluding and the closest House races being decided, we now have a clearer picture of Democrats' dominant midterms.

Some 56% of people cast votes for Democrats in House races, compared to 42% who voted Republican. That's a 14-point spread on the House ballot.

It's the biggest win for either party in 50 years , since after Watergate.

Democrats' wins in 2018 and 2006 — the earlier of which then-President George W. Bush described as a "thumping" — and the 2010 "shellacking" that Democrats took, as former President Barack Obama called it, were all less-than-10-point House margins. Obama's 2008 election comes the closest at almost 11 points.

So far, Democrats have flipped 46 House seats currently held by Republicans.

That number could rise to 49, as Democrats lead in three other races that have not yet been called.

It's the second-most number of flipped seats this century. The first was in 2010 when Republicans flipped 66 seats, netting 64, a backlash to the passage of the Affordable Care Act, which has since become more popular.

This year's drubbing was so resounding that when all the votes are counted, Democrats will likely have the largest majority in Congress since the early 1990s .

national.title: Dozens missing after boat carrying migrants sinks off Senegal's coast
national.summary: At least four bodies have been recovered from the boat which was reportedly carrying between 50 and 100 people.
national.body:
Senegalese authorities are continuing search operations after a boat said to be carrying between 50 and 100 migrants capsized in the Atlantic Ocean.

Four bodies have reportedly been recovered so far. Dozens of people are still missing.

Personal belongings were found on the badly damaged boat, which washed ashore near the village of Yenne, south of Dakar. Search operations continued throughout Wednesday and were due to resume on Thursday.

This comes less than two weeks after a shipwreck off the coast of the north-western town of Thieppe killed at least 39 people, in one of Senegal's deadliest migration disasters.

Oumar Sow, a representative of the village chief, said the latest tragedy happened around 02:00 local time (02:00 GMT).

"Cries could be heard coming from the pirogue that were audible even from the beach," the AFP news agency quoted him as saying.

A survivor questioned by the police said there were about 100 people on the boat, including five women, AFP reported.

However, a local official told Reuters news agency it was carrying 50 people, adding that the boat hit a rock as migrants were transferring from small fishing boats to a larger vessel.

national.body:
Michelle L. Price, Associated Press Michelle L. Price, Associated Press

E. Eduardo Castillo, Associated Press E. Eduardo Castillo, Associated Press

SHENZHEN, China (AP) — For President Donald Trump, the meeting with the leaders of two other nuclear powers -- China's Xi Jinping and Russia's Vladimir Putin -- was supposed to be a diplomatic triumph: It would serve as proof that Trump could negotiate with two of America's toughest rivals.

WATCH: Trump lands in China for trade talks and high-stakes summit with Xi and Putin

Before the trio met Thursday in a villa in the Chinese tech hub of Shenzhen, the U.S. president sought to flatter both Xi and Putin as his friends. They were to discuss the wars in Ukraine and Iran and how to reduce the dangers posed by nuclear arsenals.

But after roughly 70 minutes behind closed doors, they agreed to a far narrower agenda. They would like to reform the United Nations, refine more fossil fuels and curb the reach of the International Criminal Court.

What was billed as a historic trilateral meeting in the end looked like a fleeting photo op. Trump quickly left the villa and boarded Air Force One without saying a word to reporters about his time with Xi and Putin.

Fiona, the Cincinnati Zoo's famed hippo, underwent a colonoscopy this week, and now veterinarians are trying a new way to help her pass a knit cap that she swallowed after it slipped into her enclosure.

The zoo's animal care team borrowed a vibration plate from a horse farm, hoping the shaking will help move things along through her digestive tract, the zoo said Wednesday.

Video released by the zoo Wednesday shows Fiona snorting and moving about her indoor enclosure.

Veterinarians sedated her Tuesday for a second time to evaluate her condition, said Mike Wenninger, the zoo's director of animal health.

An ultrasound showed some bunching of her intestines, indicating she is still trying to pass the obstruction, Wenninger said. They also conducted a colonoscopy, using a 9-foot scope, he said.

national.body: South Florida communities are reeling in the aftermath of widespread flooding that forced evacuations and school closures this week, as residents braced for additional rainfall on Thursday. Flood watches remained in effect through Thursday night for major metropolitan areas like Miami, Fort Lauderdale and Palm Beach, according to the National Weather Service.Parts of Florida's Broward County, which includes Fort Lauderdale and the nearby coastal city of Hollywood, have received more than 15 inches of rain since Tuesday, and up to a foot of rain has fallen in other areas. Photos and video footage show neighborhoods completely inundated, with residential properties and numerous vehicles partially submerged in water.Fort Lauderdale Fire Rescue shared multiple videos to social media that captured its crew members either driving or wading on foot through knee-high waters. In several of them, rescuers were seen collecting debris and approaching vehicles that had become stranded on flooded roads.One video, shared by X user Sruly Meyer, showed floodwaters rushing over a Hollywood street where his Uber was driving. The water appeared to create small waves that lapped against tree trunks and inched up the surrounding driveways. "Insane flooding. Uber to airport," Meyer captioned the video. Law enforcement officers have been conducting rescues since Wednesday in particularly hard-hit locations. Officers with the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission said they rescued more than 70 residents, in addition to 20 or 30 pets, from a flooded Hollywood apartment complex on Wednesday, CBS Miami reported. national.summary: Democratic Sen. Tim Kaine says he will force a vote on the Senate floor in the coming weeks to require President Donald Trump's administration to calculate the human rights consequences of its policies in Russia.
national.body:
Mary Clare Jalonick, Associated Press Mary Clare Jalonick, Associated Press

WASHINGTON (AP) — Democratic Sen. Tim Kaine says he will force a vote on the Senate floor in the coming weeks to require President Donald Trump's administration to calculate the human rights consequences of its policies in Russia.

Kaine is introducing the resolution on Thursday under an arcane provision of a foreign policy law that allows any senator to trigger a vote requiring a report on a country's human rights practices. His measure would request more information about the effects of a diesel deal with Russia that was struck by the Republican president in October and that waived sanctions against Moscow and allowed for the sale of millions of tons of the fuel.

The measure would also require the State Department to report on the consequences of other U.S. policies as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said that the Pentagon delayed the delivery of Patriot air defense interceptors and that U.S. intelligence that warns of incoming Russian attacks against his country had been interrupted.

Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News

Trump said in announcing the deal on Oct. 9 that Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel, followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons "immediately thereafter." Russia will deliver an additional 3 million tons "within a short period of time" after that, he wrote on social media. He did not address the sanctions or Russia's war but said, "Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my Greatest Priority."

If passed, the resolution would ask the State Department to calculate how Trump's policies have affected Russia's ability to wage war in Ukraine and if they have caused or worsened human rights abuses. It also asks for an update on the current status of negotiations to end the war, which Russia launched in February 2022.

Kaine says he hopes the resolution, which he calls a "test of good faith," can pass with bipartisan votes.

national.summary: Anthropic decided to barrel ahead with the IPO despite jitters among some investors over market volatility, a potential regulatory crackdown by a Democratic-led Congress next year and growing anti-AI sentiment among the public.
national.body:
Barbara Ortutay, Associated Press Barbara Ortutay, Associated Press

NEW YORK (AP) — The artificial intelligence giant Anthropic opened for trading Thursday in the biggest public stock offering ever, despite investor fears of a possible AI bubble and public anxiety that the technology threatens lives and livelihoods.

Anthropic shares began trading at $111.50, spiking more than 30% above the initial public offering price.

The company priced its IPO at $83 per share, enough to value the entire business at $1.5 trillion, surpassing SpaceX as the largest IPO on record.

Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News

The price was surprising high given investor worries had ratcheted up even more recently following the stunning ouster of AI's chief promoter, the CEO of Nvidia, amid a possible Chinese spying scandal. Anthropic had earlier set a much lower price range between $70 to $78 per share.

"It's a big win for the tech sector after a white-knuckle time with Nvidia," said Dan Ives, a financial analyst at Yorkville Ives & Co. "The pricing shows strong demand among investors."

A big test remains if investors maintain the classic "IPO pop" by keeping the stock aloft in its first day — or if it will tumble by the close.

national.title: Venezuela signs military deal with US less than a year after Maduro's removal
national.summary: The US Secretary of Defence says Venezuela has "gone from our most aggressive regional threat to a compliant security partner".
national.body:
The United States and Venezuela have re-established military ties less than a year after US forces seized the then-leader of the South American country, Nicolás Maduro, in a raid on the capital, Caracas.

The interim government led by Delcy Rodríguez, Maduro's former vice-president, signed a military co-operation agreement with US Secretary of Defence Pete Hegseth on Wednesday.

Few details about the deal have been released so far but Hegseth said that Venezuela had "gone from our most aggressive regional threat to a compliant security partner" in less than 12 months.

Interim President Rodríguez said the deal would help confront "common threats".

Military co-operation between the two countries was terminated in 2005 by Hugo Chávez, Venezuela's left-wing president at the time.

Chávez alleged that US military personnel sent to Venezuela to train their counterparts had made disparaging remarks about his government.

He also accused the US military office located in Fuerte Tiuna, Venezuela's largest military complex, of being "an organ of the CIA... conspiring against the government".

Under Nicolás Maduro, who succeeded Chávez after the latter's death from cancer, relations between the two countries deteriorated further.

national.title: Putin vows 'far more painful' response to Ukraine's strikes on Crimean Bridge
national.summary: The bridge - a symbol of Russia's occupation of the Crimean Peninsula - suffered major damaged following a combined attack by Ukraine earlier this week.
national.body:
Moscow's retaliation for attacks on the Crimean Bridge will be "far more painful" than Kyiv's strikes, Vladimir Putin has vowed.

In the early hours of Thursday, the double-arched, 12-mile bridge connecting Russia to Ukraine's occupied peninsula of Crimea was hit for a third time this week.

A combined missile-and-drone strike on Tuesday destroyed the central road section of the bridge, collapsing part of it into the water and rendering it unusable for road traffic.

But at a press conference after historic talks with his Chinese and US counterparts in Shenzhen, Russian president Putin said Moscow's response would be even more significant.

Putin claimed the bridge was used exclusively for civilian purposes and not to transport military equipment, as Kyiv has alleged, or petroleum products.

Since illegally annexing the Crimean Peninsula in 2014, Moscow has used it as a military base, with airbases, troop concentrations, training grounds and artillery stockpiles.

From there it has also carried out strikes on the rest of the country and resupplied its troops in southern Ukraine.

Commenting on the strikes on the bridge, Kyiv's defence ministry said that for Ukraine, they amounted to to "time gained and lives saved. The less that reaches the occupiers, the less hits our warriors."

national.title: US consortium wins huge Kenya mining deal, beating Chinese rivals
national.summary: The Mrima Hill site is estimated to hold deposits of critical minerals worth more than $60bn (£45bn).
national.body:
A US-led consortium, Frontier Minerals, has won the tender to develop Kenya's Mrima Hill mining project, beating seven bidders, including companies from China and Australia.

The site is estimated to hold deposits of critical minerals worth more than $60bn (£45bn), including niobium, used in electric vehicles, aerospace and defence technology.

Frontier Minerals says its proposal aims to keep more of the economic benefits in Kenya through "processing and refining of minerals in-country".

The deal comes as Washington seeks greater access to Africa's minerals, aiming to strengthen US supply chains and compete with China.

Frontier Minerals brings together three US companies - Bunker Hill Mining Corp, American Resources Corporation and ReElement Technologies Corporation. The consortium combines expertise in mineral resource development, critical materials supply chains and advanced refining technologies.

A central part of its proposal is to develop mineral processing and refining capacity in Kenya. Brad Barnett from Frontier Minerals said the company wanted the country to capture more value from its mineral resources.

Mrima Hill is located in Kwale County, near Kenya's Indian Ocean coastline. The site covers about 390 acres of forest.

The prospect of mining in the area has raised concerns among local residents, who fear the project could damage the forest and threaten their ancestral heritage.

Chautauqua County Executive PJ Wendel has reaffirmed his commitment to revitalizing the former NRG Power Plant in Dunkirk following his attendance at the 2026 Advanced Nuclear NY Summit, which was Tuesday and Wednesday, in Rochester.

During the event, Gov. Kathy Hochul announced the completion of New York State’s Advanced Nuclear Master Plan, a comprehensive roadmap outlining the State’s goal of developing five gigawatts of new nuclear power generation. The plan identifies opportunities for advanced nuclear energy development across Upstate New York, emphasizing economic growth, workforce development, energy reliability, and responsible site selection.

For Wendel, the announcement reinforces the importance of positioning the former NRG property as a potential location for future advanced nuclear energy development.

“The former NRG Power Plant represents one of the greatest opportunities for economic revitalization in Chautauqua County,” said Wendel. “I have remained committed to bringing this property back into productive use because I know what it can mean for Dunkirk and our entire region. We have the infrastructure, the workforce, and the history of energy production needed to compete for an investment of this magnitude. Now is the time to make sure Chautauqua County is part of New York’s energy future.”

The former NRG site offers several advantages for potential energy development, including established electrical grid connections, industrial-zoned property, access to Lake Erie, and a skilled regional workforce with experience in the energy sector.

Wendel emphasized that restoring productive use to the property could deliver benefits extending well beyond energy generation.

“Bringing this site back online is about creating good-paying jobs, attracting private investment, and restoring a valuable property to our tax base,” Wendel continued. “That means new opportunities for our residents, additional resources to support essential public services, and the potential to reduce the tax burden on local families and businesses. We also need to be looking at ways to expand access to reliable, affordable electricity. With utility costs continuing to strain household budgets, developing new energy resources that can help stabilize and potentially lower electricity bills must remain a priority.”

NYPA is pursuing the development of at least one gigawatt of new advanced nuclear generation in Upstate New York, an effort that forms part of the State’s broader five-gigawatt goal.

Chris Rodriguez and Kids At Promise are holding a Memorial Boxing Tournament in honor of Fredonia native Tommy Roque on Saturday at the Chautauqua County Fairgrounds. The event is a USA Amateur Boxing Sanctioned Tournament.

"I decided to host the event to give Tommy Roque his flowers," Rodriguez shared. "2XL Boxing has helped me as a Marine Corps veteran who as head of security forces served overseas with my own PTSD. Helping these kids is extremely fulfilling to my soul. After running and organizing this program for six years now I have to pay my respect to Tommy who did this for over 15 years day in and day out without much recognition.

"Currently, none of our coaches get paid to do this; we are all free volunteers. It takes a special kind of person who wants to take on the responsibility of not just helping the community but helping raise and guide other people's children away from the temptations of society. Tommy deserves to be celebrated."

When asked what he hopes to achieve with the event Rodriguez said, "My hopes are to create an event that allows people to see our local boxers flourish especially with how hard they have worked to get to this point but also I just want people to come and enjoy themselves. To enjoy the company of others in the community for a couple hours. With everything going on in the world sometimes we forget how beautiful and blessed we are in Dunkirk, NY to have such a close-knit community where everyone knows each other."

The event is $20 with a $25 ringside upgrade. It begins at 3 p.m. with matches beginning 4. There will be basket raffles as well as a 50-50 drawing. All proceeds will go to 2XL Boxing, a program started by Roque, who died in August. Already, $1,000 was donated by Juan Rivera to pay for trophies, and his Spanish food truck El Rincon Criollo will be there as well.

Mel Santiago is doing photography, local restaurant owner Eddie Diaz will be on hand to DJ. Ring announcing will be done by local influencer and singer King Taco. Firehouse Subs is donating food for the coaches and boxers and The Nook has pledged $500 to the event and is volunteering as well. The door prize has been given by Jim Kelly and the Kelly for Kids Foundation, a signed Riddell Mini Helmet and book.

Some of Roque's 2XL program kids who went on to become Pro Boxers include Ivan Hernandez who now runs Top Level Boxing in Jamestown; Tommy Roque Jr. who is in the Marine Corps Boxing Hall of Fame and a two-time Armed Forces Champion; Gueirrmo Sanchez who started off 11-0 as a pro; Wilfredo Flores who became the WBA-Fedecentro Lightweight Champion of the World and Elon DeJesus who is currently ranked 11th in the United States and 82nd in the world with a 12-1-2 record. All started as local Dunkirk 2XL Boxing youth.

local.body: BUFFALO, N.Y. (WIVB) -- FeedMore Western New York unveiled its new $115 million headquarters and distribution center in Hamburg on Thursday. FeedMore opened its new 200,000-square-foot facility, which is located on Camp Road. The expanded space -- which was supported by more than $53 million in funding from New York State -- will consolidate the nonprofit's operations into a single, specialized campus. FeedMore WNY previously had two separate sites in Buffalo; the new site is more than twice the size of the previous warehouses. “No New Yorker should ever have to worry about where their next meal is coming from, and this transformative facility ensures that FeedMore WNY has the modern infrastructure needed to serve our community for generations,” Hochul said. "And I want to make sure that we don't have that situation." The new facility features a 50-foot-tall warehouse that leaves room for future expansion, specialized forklifts, as well as a high racking system. A new commercial commissary space will make up to 20,000 meals per day -- which doubles FeedMore's current potential output. The facility will initially have around 160 paid employees, with that number expected to increase in the future. It also will allow FeedMore to double its volunteer capacity. "For years, our critical mission was restricted by the physical boundaries of our old facilities. Today, we step into a larger, unified campus that fully empowers us to alleviate hunger, expand our RISE workforce development program and tackle the root causes of food insecurity throughout Erie, Niagara, Cattaraugus and Chautauqua counties," FeedMore WNY President and CEO Tara Ellis said. local.body:
Listen • 2:23 Folk-rock musician Adam Henne typically plays at local clubs and record shops. But on a recent Saturday morning, he was strumming his acoustic guitar at Lollypop Farm.

"Word has gotten around that it's soothing and pleasant for the animals who have to wait here in cages to have some pleasant background music," he said. "So, the call went out to musicians around Rochester to come and lend a hand, and I think a lot of us are excited to do that."

Henne's audience was a roomful of cats. A scared looking red tabby wearing a surgical cone slowly peered over the top of the box he was perched in.

"A little quiet acoustic music maybe is a nice way to let the cats know that we're not threatening and this is a safe place," Henne said, after noticing that the cat, Jack, was frightened.

Music has the power to move us and soothe us and animals are not immune to its magic. That's the philosophy behind Lollypop Farm ' s new venture with Wild Tunes, a Houston-based nonprofit devoted to enriching the lives of homeless pets.

Wild Tunes was founded in 2023 by Yuvi Agarwal, a 10-year-old animal lover and musician who saw how his music calmed his dog.

"Animals who are coming into this space are often dealing with a lot of change, a lot of uncertainty, and that leads to anxiety," noted Sydney Jenkins, Lollypop Farm's director of humane education.

The hope, she said, is that live music will provide relief for the anxiety and a safe, comforting human connection.

Rand Aerospace & Defense Group's plans to add a second factory in the southern end of the county are moving ahead.

The Chautauqua County Industrial Development Agency approved financial assistance for a $5.22 million expansion plan for Rand, as it purchases the former Serta Mattress factory in the town of Ellicott.

According to Rosemarie Strandburg with the county IDA, this second location will allow Rand to not only keep its current 115 employees but add an additional 31 employees over the next three years.

"This expansion represents an important next chapter for Rand as we continue to grow our capabilities and respond to increasing demand from our customers," Dan McKenrick, president and CEO of Rand Aerospace & Defense Group said in a statement after the meeting. "Our investment in this new facility will provide the additional manufacturing capacity needed to support our existing and future programs, while creating new opportunities for our employees and the local workforce. We are proud to continue investing in Chautauqua County and appreciate the support of the CCIDA and our local partners."

McKenrick first approached the county IDA publicly about Rand purchasing the former Serta Mattress located at 2375 Parkway Drive in October. At that meeting, he credited the county IDA for helping Rand solidify in the past, which is allowing them to be able to expand.

"Supporting the growth of established manufacturers like Rand is a key part of our economic development strategy," said Mark Geise, deputy county executive for economic development and the chief executive officer for the county IDA. "This project represents a significant private-sector investment that will increase manufacturing capacity, retain more than 100 existing jobs, and create additional employment opportunities. local.title: State moving forward with nuclear plans
local.summary: New York state Gov. Kathy Hochul has announced the completion of the Master Plan for Responsible Advanced Nuclear Development in New York (Advanced Nuclear Master Plan). Demonstrating New York’s leadership role in the national effort to develop new nuclear energy, the Master Plan is a comprehensive
local.body:
New York state Gov. Kathy Hochul has announced the completion of the Master Plan for Responsible Advanced Nuclear Development in New York (Advanced Nuclear Master Plan). Demonstrating New York's leadership role in the national effort to develop new nuclear energy, the Master Plan is a comprehensive statewide roadmap to achieve the Governor's Nuclear Reliability Backbone to create five gigawatts (GW) of new nuclear power.

Co-authored by the New York State Energy Research Development Authority (NYSERDA) and the New York State Department of Public Service (DPS), and unveiled today at the State's third Nuclear Summit in Rochester, the master plan outlines coordinated state actions to support the safe and timely development and deployment of advanced nuclear power plants in upstate New York.

"Expanding emission-free, round-the-clock nuclear power is a cornerstone of my all-of-the-above approach to ensure we have enough energy to keep the lights on and costs down for New Yorkers," Hochul said. "The completed Advanced Nuclear Master Plan can serve as a national model by pairing our ambitious target of five gigawatts of new nuclear generation with a comprehensive strategy to support thoughtful development and deployment of what will be the largest buildout the country has seen in more than three decades."

Dunkirk's former NRG plant, now owned by Genover, could be a candidate for this type of power generation. It was one of eight communities to express an interest in the opportunity in 2025.

The master plan was developed in response to Hochul's 2025 directive to establish a framework supporting advanced nuclear energy development in New York. Now, the master plan will help facilitate the development of the Nuclear Reliability Backbone, which Governor Hochul directed the creation of in her 2026 State of the State, that will add 5 gigawatts of new nuclear generation to the 3.4 gigawatts already in existence.

DPS today also issued a White Paper with policy recommendations to help enable the commercial viability of advanced nuclear development, potential cost reductions and other considerations for advancing the Governor's Nuclear Reliability Backbone.

In addition, the New York Power Authority (NYPA) also continues to move forward to develop and construct at least one gigawatt of nuclear energy in Upstate New York.

Public Service Commission Chair Rory Christian said, "The Master Plan and White Paper announced today offer actionable next steps to safely and responsibly facilitate the development of 5 gigawatts of new nuclear in New York State. Thanks to the leadership of Governor Hochul, these collaborative and comprehensive interagency workstreams serve as a strong foundation to expand New York's nuclear footprint to maintain a reliable grid while centering community input and workforce opportunities."

local.body:
CRANBERRY TOWNSHIP, Pa. -- It took Kyle Dubas more than three years, but the Pittsburgh Penguins general manager finally said the quiet part out loud.

Asked Wednesday what gives him hope that his struggling team, which is mired near the bottom of the Eastern Conference and has three regulation wins through 20 games, can turn it around in time to salvage this season, Dubas turned philosophical.

Yes, making the playoffs for a second straight year would be nice. Yet that’s not the metric he will lean on to gauge progress.

Dubas would like the team’s younger players to take “major steps.” He’d like to see the iconic, aging core led by captain Sidney Crosby show it still has “gas left in the tank.” He’d like some of the prospects he’s acquired since taking over to make a push for NHL playing time.

If those things can happen, Dubas believes the franchise will be on “the right track” regardless of where the Penguins wind up in the standings.

Then, Dubas finished by using a phrase that included the one word he has consistently avoided uttering publicly since taking over in the summer of 2023.

“This has been, I think rightfully, an unorthodox style of rebuilding a team because of the players that are here,” he said.

local.summary: If there is one thing the midterm elections decided nationally, it was this. Americans want a better system of checks and balances. How else do you describe the massive turnover in both the House of Representatives and U.S. Senate? Democrats last gained nine or more Senate seats in a midterm electio
local.body:
If there is one thing the midterm elections decided nationally, it was this. Americans want a better system of checks and balances.

How else do you describe the massive turnover in both the House of Representatives and U.S. Senate?

Democrats last gained nine or more Senate seats in a midterm election in 1958, during Republican President Dwight Eisenhower's second term. That year, Democrats wrested away 13 Republican-held seats and also won both of Alaska's newly created seats, for a total gain of 15 seats.

Former Rep. Mary Peltola's victory in the controversial Alaska race gave Democrats a 56-44 majority when the new Congress begins in January, marking the party's largest advantage in the Senate in 16 years. Democrats held 58 Senate seats in the waning days of the 111th Congress, which concluded on Jan. 3, 2011.

"Fifty-six seats was an unimaginable result even just a few months ago,” Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer said in a statement posted on social media. “Most people didn't think 51 Democratic Senate seats was a possibility at the beginning of this cycle."

Even without Alaska, Democrats would have secured their largest majority since January 2015, when Republicans took control after flipping nine Democratic seats in the 2014 midterms during President Barack Obama's second term.

As for readers, many in this region who did vote Republican in local elections, 53% in response to our poll question, "Are you pleased with the national election results?" said no while 47% said "yes."

local.body:
While it was Allegany-Limestone/Hinsdale that won the league title with a 9-0-1 record, third-place Jamestown garnered a majority of the postseason awards in Chautauqua-Cattaraugus Athletic Association Division I boys soccer this season.

Red & Green junior Beckett Lumia was named the All-Conference Player of the Year, senior Aaden Howard was named the league's Defensive Player of the Year and senior Caden Wahl was Jamestown's Individual Sportsmanship Award winner as the team was also recognized. Also, Jamestown's Bonnie Schnars was named the Coach of the Year after the Red & Green finished 7-3-0 in the division.

Lumia scored 14 goals and added four assists while Howard had one assist while anchoring a defense that allowed 43 goals on the season. Joining them on the First Team was junior Robbie Williams, who had three goals and two assists.

The league-champion Gators had four players on the First Team. Junior midfielder Collin Coleman had 16 goals and five assists, freshman midfielder Colten Wilczewski had two goals and an assist, sophomore defender Adam Jaquith had two goals and three assists while anchoring a defense that allowed just 18 goals on the season, and senior goalkeeper Donovan Booker helped the Gators post 11 clean sheets.

Second-place Southwestern had a pair of players recognized on the First Team. Junior forward Wilson Genareo had 16 goals and three assists while junior midfielder Matthew Persia had eight goals and four assists.

Olean had three players honored on the First Team. Senior forward Connor Hogle had 23 goals and three assists, senior midfielder Ethan Woodring had eight assists and junior defender Gehrig Perry anchored a defense that allowed 52 goals against.

Dunkirk senior midfielder Brady Dobek was named the league's Offensive Player of the Year after tallying eight goals and 12 assists. He was joined on the First Team by senior midfielder Lucas Felt, who had six goals and five assists, and junior defender Brendan Worczak, who anchored a defense that allowed 45 goals against.

Allegany-Limestone/Hinsdale had three players named to the Second Team in sophomore forward Owen Buzzard (14 goals, two assists), senior defender Colton Reska and junior defender Hunter Cassidy (one assist).

local.body: Chants of ‘We want justice’ rang throughout Niagara Falls, as the family and friends of Jayla Brown and Jalin Rios demanded answers as to why nobody has been arrested for killing their loved ones.It has been over four months since 19-year-old Jayla Brown and 22-year-old Jalin Rios were shot and killed at Fourth of July gatherings in Niagara Falls.The two were killed in separate shootings on the same day. Their mothers, Carretha Brown and Celis Rios, say the lack of an arrest by the Niagara Falls Police Department has only angered the families and added to their grief.“We lost our son, and nobody has been accountable for his death,” Celis said.“We need answers. We want everything to come out right now,” Jalin’s dad Jason said.“Absolutely hell. No one contacts me, no updates, no nothing. If I don't reach out, I don't hear from anyone,” Brown said. We need answers for these unsolved murders, these homicides. We need answers, and we need them to be more diligent about solving these murders.”Together, the Rios and Brown families led a march of a few hundred people down Main Street, from the Niagara Falls Police Department to City Hall.The group carried pictures and signs of both Jalin and Jayla, and they chanted ‘We want justice’ for not just their own loved ones, but for all those killed in Niagara Falls, who have seen their investigations go cold.“They keep saying the same thing. entertainment.title: ‘I Play Rocky’ Stars Unite With Original ‘Rocky’ Producer for Film’s 50th Anniversary Celebration
entertainment.summary: Irwin Winkler, who was behind Sylvester Stallone's 1976 hit, joined Anthony Ippolito, AnnaSophia Robb and director Peter Farrelly at the Academy Museum event.
entertainment.body:
Rocky minds old and new came together on Tuesday night for a 50th anniversary celebration of Sylvester Stallone ‘s breakout 1976 hit.

The iconic boxing movie is back in the culture not only for its milestone anniversary but also because of I Play Rocky , which chronicles Stallone’s journey of bringing his project to the big screen. At the event — held at the Academy Museum — I Play Rocky stars Anthony Ippolito , AnnaSophia Robb, P.J. Byrne and Kiki Seto, director Peter Farrelly and writer Peter Gamble were all in attendance, alongside Rocky producer Irwin Winkler . (They also stopped by a THR photo studio inside of Fanny’s restaurant, with images below.) Related Stories Lifestyle THR Celebrates Hollywood's New Wave of Stars at Next Gen Dinner Movies The Sound of Rocky: How an Anthem Was Born

Winkler took the stage for a Q&A before the special screening of Rocky , recalling how Stallone came in for a meeting and mentioned the story he had in mind. “He said he would write the story very quickly, with the understanding that if we liked the script, we had to star him in the film,” Winkler remembered of the star’s comments to him and fellow producer Robert Chartoff. “And the rest you’ll see on I Play Rocky . It really told the story very, very well, probably better than I could.”

The producer added that “we made this little movie for a million dollars, we didn’t expect anything out of it” but credits its uplifting message — following the Vietnam War and Watergate where “people were really kind of down and depressed” — for its success. “This movie came along and said, ‘America is also a place if you believe in yourself, you have the opportunity to succeed.’ And I think, in a strange way, I think we’re back to some of the same feelings,” Winkler said. “I think what I Play Rocky shows you is the story about a man who believes in himself, that America can give you that opportunity to succeed. I don’t want to sound political but I can’t help it.”

Winkler also touched on the spinoff Creed films, saying “We thought we had put the franchise to bed with Rocky Balboa ” but upon meeting Ryan Coogler, “he had the same passion that Stallone had shown 40 years before” and “I said to myself, ‘If we’re going to ever make another Rocky , I want to make it with this young Ryan Coogler.'”

Midway through the conversation, Winkler was joined by Farrelly and Ippolito; the filmmaker recalled watching Rocky as a freshman in college and “I remember walking out of the theater, being like, ‘Woo, woo!’ And I didn’t know what I was wooing about, but I was pumped up — to do what? I have no idea. But I was inspired, and I remember going back to school and getting my buddies and being like, ‘OK, you’ve got to see this movie.’ The closest I could compare it to is like having a sports team. It was like you fell in love with a sports team, and you were rooting for him, and Rocky was our team.”

E. Lockhart, the author turned showrunner behind Prime Video’s hit We Were Liars , will adapt the trilogy into a series, serving as writer and executive producer.

entertainment.title: Parker Posey Knows Career Highs and Lows. Right Now, She’s Having a Blast
entertainment.summary: The indie legend, Emmy nominee and ‘Wild Horse Nine’ scene-stealer gets candid about money troubles, industry sexism and the wildest press tour of her career: “I just got a publicist.”
entertainment.body:
“I’ve never done anything like this,” Parker Posey says. She has certainly, over her singular 35-year screen career, sat down with journalists plenty, and likely on this very couch at the Chateau Marmont, where she’s been staying over a busy weekend of events in Los Angeles. But our meeting has come on the heels of a dizzying press run for Posey, one that feels as much about her entire life onscreen as it is about her fresh projects that are ripe for promotion — most significantly, her small but vivid role in Martin McDonagh ’s new Oscar-bound film, Wild Horse Nine .

“I don’t really have a reference point to this because I just got a publicist a few years ago,” Posey says, between sips of her grapefruit juice. While the sustained exposure — the periods of talking about oneself, really — could seem daunting, you sense quickly that Posey approaches it like she does anything else. She excitedly orders olives and almonds and crudité for our lounge table. She happily ignores our time limit, even if she’ll have to hail an Uber across town to meet some friends for lunch. She makes strong, direct eye contact, constantly shifting between my questions and her own curiosity about the person sitting before her. “I bet we have friends in common,” she says at one point. Related Stories TV 'My Favorite Murder' HBO Series Sets December Premiere Lifestyle John Malkovich Sets West End Return With Rosalind Eleazar in 'History'

There’s nobody like Parker Posey, and this has been true for a long time across movies and TV. It’s why she remains so synonymous with the great American indie-film run of the ‘90s, why she can now both go viral with a single scream of a line — see recent HBO examples in The Staircase and, of course, The White Lotus — and still imbue the dialogue with surprising, heartfelt depth. And it’s perhaps why, as Posey finally, really puts herself out there, there’s a lot of love coming her way. You’ll see it in the thrill of her pulling out a title at random in the Criterion Closet, selecting Ghost World , and cheering, “I love this movie — yay!” Or in the warmth of her reviving her old bond with CBS Sunday Mornings correspondent Mo Rocca, as they quote Katharine Hepburn back and forth, grinning ear to ear.

“You’re 15 again, at North Carolina School of the Arts with your gay bestie — well, we didn’t say that [term] then,” Posey says of being interviewed by Rocca for that plum segment. “It was so meaningful to me. Because you’re always going to feel the same — you’ll just keep getting older. And it’s true, I do still feel the same. I feel like that person, excited to be at NCSA with Maurice.”

entertainment.title: Brothers Osborne & Cody Johnson Celebrate Teen Rebellion in ‘Born And Raised Hell’: ‘It’s Kind of Our Story as a Town’
entertainment.summary: Billboard's Makin' Tracks looks at the writing and recording behind the Brothers Osborne and Cody Johnson collab "Born and Raised Hell."
entertainment.body:
Not just because it features a Country Music Association male vocalist of the year winner, though having Cody Johnson as a guest deserves high fives.

But even more than that, for discerning listeners looking for clues in the song’s parade of youthful misdeeds and rabble-rousing, “Born and Raised Hell” contains shards of the Osborne’s upbringing on the Atlantic Coast in Deale, Md. That was, in fact, part of the mission as they built their new album, Watertown , released Oct. 23. Explore Brothers Osborne Cody Johnson See latest videos, charts and news

“We did want to have those more specific items in the album, things that really anchored it back to our hometown,” says lead singer T.J. Osborne. “I feel like we’ve spent so many years writing, and trying to write, songs for everybody [else], as one does. You tend to leave out a lot of specificity.” Related Underscores Is First Transgender Woman Nominated for Best Dance/Electronic Recording Grammy Ella Langley Becomes First Act to Earn Top Two of TouchTunes Frontline Chart El Coyote Earns Third Regional Mexican Airplay No. 1 With 'Ranchero Enamorado'

That personal detail arrives in the new single, “Born and Raised Hell,” through two aquatic references: swimming out to the jetty and sitting on the bank of Rockhold Creek. The creek is a real place, and Brothers Osborne wouldn’t be quite the same without the experiences they racked up there.

“Where we grew up specifically was where Rockhold Creek opened up into the Chesapeake Bay,” guitarist John Osborne says. “Right at the end of Rockhold Creek is a very long jetty that helps break up the waves and the tide that comes into the creek, because there are a lot of marinas and a lot of businesses [near] the creek. We grew up right there on the end — almost right at the point of it, where that big jetty is. We would just get into all sorts of trouble right there on the on the banks of the Chesapeake.”

When John wrote the new single at his East Nashville studio, he conveyed the desire to address the Osbornes’ homegrown history to co-writers Kendell Marvel (“Right Where I Need to Be,” “Either Way”) and Lee Thomas Miller (“In Color,” “It Ain’t My Fault”). Marvel scrolled through his phone for an appropriate title and found “Born and Raised Hell,” an idea that Miller assumed was already in circulation somewhere. They couldn’t find any competition online; the only other song with that name in the performing rights organizations’ databases appears to be unrecorded.

entertainment.body:
The Hollywood Reporter hosted its Next Gen dinner, presented by Meta, on Wednesday night, celebrating the magazine’s recent lists of fast-rising stars everyone is fighting to cast and 35 rising Hollywood executives under 35 on the rooftop of the new Public West Hollywood.

Sophie Nélisse , Charlie Hall and Keyla Monterroso Mejia came out to represent this year’s Next Gen talent group, alongside Widow’s Bay ‘s Kingston Rumi Southwick, The Pitt ‘s Supriya Ganesh and The Body stars Shirley Chen, Sofia Wylie, Kristina Bogic, Geena Meszaros, Sara Boustany and Bella Neuspiel (plus creator Quinn Shephard and showrunner Gina Gammell). The evening began with cocktails and mingling on the roof, with Nélisse, Hall and Mejia taking a moment to pose together with their individual covers. Guests also stopped by the Meta Ray-Ban glasses try-on station, with each attendee receiving a pair that they could set up on the spot.

After some tray-passed apps and plenty of red carpet photos, everyone found their seats for the dinner portion of the evening. THR senior entertainment reporter Mia Galuppo offered up some brief remarks, telling the group how “we started this issue over 30 years ago with the idea that we are going to tap the future leaders of Hollywood,” with Donna Langley, Kevin Feige and Ari Emanuel among that early Next Gen exec crop. For the last decade THR has also done the in-front-of-the-camera list, as Galuppo noted, “It’s something that we take very seriously. We base it on our own tastes as well as our reporting, talking to executives in the industry about who they’re excited about and who audiences are excited about.”

Claudine Cazian, director of strategic partnerships at Meta, noted the company wanted “to highlight and spotlight together the freshest faces and the boldest voices that are reshaping the industry” and joked “looking around this room tonight, I am both energized and inspired and slightly jealous of the collagen in everybody’s cheekbones. Appreciate it while you have it — it goes, my friends.”

“What you do and what you give to all of us, it opens hearts, it opens minds, and what you do is push culture forward and that’s not easy to do,” she continued. “Sometimes it can even be scary, so we want to thank you collectively for your craft, for your time, for your energy, for your talent and for your voice,” as the guests raised their glasses. entertainment.title: Ryan Seacrest, 51, busts out yoga poses live on ‘Wheel of Fortune’ as he shares new fitness journey
